918.title: Along the Rhine
918.hook: Jewish communities grow in German and French towns along the Rhine
918.howItsDone: Ashkenazi Jews trace their customs and prayer rite to the medieval communities of the German and French lands, and the old Jewish sites of Speyer, Worms and Mainz are visited and remembered today.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Italy and Byzantium: Jews in Rome before the arch was built, and Greek-speaking Jews across the east. Your line was old communities. Did you find out how old one place near you is? Today we follow a road north. Day nine hundred eighteen.

A river barge drifts down the Rhine, past vineyards on the slopes and the towers of cathedral towns. On board are bolts of cloth, barrels of wine, and a few merchants who stop work every Friday before dark. Where the boat ties up, in towns like Speyer, Worms and Mainz, small Jewish quarters have taken root: a synagogue, a ritual bath, a study house, a cemetery on the edge of town. Families who will one day be called Ashkenazi Jews are starting out here. And the name they come to carry was not invented on the Rhine. It comes from a single line in Genesis.
screen: `A BARGE ON THE RHINE.` → `SPEYER, WORMS, MAINZ.` → `A NAME FROM GENESIS.`

segments.voice: Open Genesis chapter ten, the long list of nations after the flood. Among the grandsons of Japheth, the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation lists the sons of Gomer: "Ashkenaz, and Riphath, and Togarmah." That's it. Ashkenaz is one name in a family tree, with no story attached. But medieval Jews read those lists as a map of the world, and they gave the old biblical names to the lands around them. Ashkenaz came to mean the German lands, and the Jews who lived there became Ashkenazim. A name from the edge of a genealogy became the name of a whole branch of the Jewish people. Now the towns themselves. Speyer, Worms and Mainz each had a Hebrew name, and the first letters of those Hebrew names were put together into one word: Shum. The three communities worked closely enough that people spoke of them as a single unit. Their leaders met, their scholars taught each other's students, and their rulings traveled from one to the next along the river. Where did their learning come from? Tradition says a scholarly family from Lucca in Italy was brought north to Mainz, and their descendants became teachers and poets there. That is the thread from yesterday: learning traveled over the Alps. These were small places. A merchant community in a Christian town lived by charters, permissions from a local bishop or ruler that could be granted and could be taken away. Life could be good, and then suddenly it was not. We will come back to the dangers. For now, hold onto the quiet first picture: a study house on a river bank, students copying, families keeping the Sabbath in a cold northern winter.
screen: `ASHKENAZ: A NAME IN GENESIS.` · then, large: `ASHKENAZ, AND RIPHATH, AND TOGARMAH.` · `SHUM: SPEYER, WORMS, MAINZ.` · `LEARNING CARRIED NORTH FROM ITALY.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: think about where your family came from. Settle, and let your breath slow. Go back as far as you know. A grandparent's town, a great-grandparent's country, or just a street. If you don't know, notice that too, gently. Was there a river, a road, a port that carried them? What did they bring with them that you still have: a word, a dish, a name? Stay with one picture of them arriving somewhere new. If you pray, you can remember them in words from your own tradition. The bell holds the time.
Ashkenaz. A name from the family tree in Genesis that medieval Jews gave to the German lands, and so to the Jews who lived there. Today's word.
Your line: the rhine communities. Today, find one thing in your life that came to you along a road or a river, and find out where it started. Day nine hundred eighteen.

919.title: Sepharad
919.hook: Jewish life in Spain under Muslim and then Christian rule
919.howItsDone: Sephardi Jews keep their own prayer rite, melodies and customs, and some families still speak or sing in Ladino, the Judeo-Spanish their ancestors carried after leaving Spain.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ashkenaz: a name from Genesis given to the German lands, and the Rhine communities of Speyer, Worms and Mainz. Your line was the rhine communities. Did you trace one thing back to where it started? Today, the other great name. Day nine hundred nineteen.

Near the end of the little book of Obadiah, one of the Prophets, there is a line about exiles from Jerusalem living in a faraway place called Sepharad. Nobody in the verse explains where that is. One word, one verse, no map. Much later, Jews living on the Iberian peninsula, in what is now Spain and Portugal, read that verse and heard their own address in it. Sepharad became the Hebrew name for Spain, and the Jews of Spain became Sephardim. Yesterday a family tree gave a name to the north. Today a prophet's line gives a name to the west. Today's word is that faraway place.
screen: `ONE VERSE IN OBADIAH.` → `A FARAWAY PLACE.` → `A NAME FOR SPAIN.`

segments.voice: Here is the line, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "the captivity of Jerusalem, that is in Sepharad." The verse itself does not say where that is, and some readers point to a city in Asia Minor. But Jewish tradition, through the Aramaic translation and the medieval commentators, heard Spain, and that reading stuck. A people far from Jerusalem found themselves named in the Bible, as exiles who still belonged to Jerusalem. Some readers hear a double feeling in that, at home and not at home, and it returns in the Sephardi story. Now the shape of that story, in two long chapters. In the first, much of Spain was ruled by Muslim dynasties, with a capital at Córdoba. Jews there spoke Arabic, read Arabic philosophy and poetry, served as doctors, translators and officials, and wrote Hebrew poetry that borrowed Arabic meters. Over the next days you will meet some of them: a courtier, a poet who led an army, a philosopher of the heart. It was not paradise. There were persecutions under some rulers, and Jews lived as a protected but lower class. But it was a long season of learning. In the second chapter, Christian kingdoms took the peninsula back, step by step. Jewish communities lived under Christian kings, again as advisers, tax collectors, doctors, and again with protection that could turn into danger. That chapter ends hard, and we will get there. Through both chapters Sephardi Jews built their own customs, prayer melodies and a language that families carried far beyond Spain: Ladino, or Judeo-Spanish. Sepharad is a place, then a memory, then a way of praying. All from one line in a little book.
screen: `THE CAPTIVITY OF JERUSALEM, THAT IS IN SEPHARAD.` · `CHAPTER ONE: UNDER MUSLIM RULE.` · `CHAPTER TWO: UNDER CHRISTIAN KINGS.` · `A PLACE, A MEMORY, A WAY OF PRAYING.`

Spanish, Ladino, Arabic, Yiddish, anything. Say it quietly, once. Notice how it sits in your mouth. Who taught it to you? Where did it travel to get to you? If you don't have one, choose a Spanish word you already know, like casa, house, and think of all the houses it has named. If you pray, you can keep the word in mind as you do. Sepharad. A place named once in Obadiah that Jewish tradition read as Spain, and so the name of the Jews of Spain and their descendants. Today's word.
Your line: spain. Today, notice one thing near you with Spanish roots, a street name, a song, a dish, and let it remind you of this long story. Day nine hundred nineteen.

920.title: Hasdai ibn Shaprut
920.hook: a Jewish physician and courtier in Córdoba who supported scholars
920.howItsDone: Jewish tradition honors those who use wealth or influence to support Torah study and protect others, and Jewish communities still raise support for schools, scholars and people in need.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sepharad: one line in Obadiah that Jewish tradition read as Spain. Your line was spain. Did something Spanish catch your ear? Today we walk into the palace at Córdoba and meet a man with access. Day nine hundred twenty.

A study house in Córdoba. The teacher asks a hard question about the law, and nobody can answer. Then a stranger sitting near the door, in ragged clothes, raises his hand and answers it perfectly. Tradition says he was a scholar who had been captured at sea and ransomed, and that before the day was out, the community wanted him as their teacher. Making that happen took money, standing, and someone close to the ruler. In Córdoba, that someone was a Jewish doctor at the caliph's court. Today, Hasdai ibn Shaprut, and what a person does with a seat near power.
screen: `A STRANGER BY THE DOOR.` → `HE ANSWERS THE QUESTION.` → `A DOCTOR AT COURT.`

segments.voice: Hasdai was a physician, and that opened the palace door. He served the caliph Abd al-Rahman the Third as a doctor, then as a diplomat and an official who handled foreign envoys and trade. A Jew in the inner circle of a Muslim ruler. Among Jews he was treated as a leader, a protector, the person you went to when a community anywhere was in trouble. What did he do with that place? Three things stand out in the stories. First, the scholar by the door. The medieval chronicler Abraham ibn Daud tells how the ransomed sage, Moses ben Hanoch, was set up as head of learning in Córdoba, and how Hasdai supported his school. For a long time, Jews in Spain had sent their hardest questions east, to the academies of Babylon. Now they could ask at home. Second, he paid for poets and grammarians. Two of them, Menahem ben Saruq and Dunash ben Labrat, got into a fierce argument about how Hebrew works, and the argument itself helped grow a whole new Hebrew poetry in Spain. Third, a letter attributed to Hasdai reaches out to a faraway king of the Khazars, who was said to rule a Jewish kingdom. Remember the Khazars. They come back soon. There is an old line from the book of Esther that fits him. Mordecai tells Queen Esther, who also had a place near a throne, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "who knoweth whether thou art not come to royal estate for such a time as this?" A seat near power is not only an honor. In this story it is a job.
screen: `A DOCTOR WHO OPENS THE PALACE DOOR.` · `A SCHOOL IN CÓRDOBA.` · `POETS, GRAMMARIANS, A LETTER.` · then, large: `FOR SUCH A TIME AS THIS.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: notice your own place. Settle, and let your breath slow. You may not sit near a king, but you have some place. A job, a group chat, a seat on a committee, a skill, a person who listens to you. Name one. Now ask quietly: who is outside that door who could use what I can reach? A student, a new neighbor, someone looking for work. Let one name or face come to mind. Keep it there. If you pray, you can hold that person in your own words. The bell holds the time.
Hasdai ibn Shaprut. A Jewish physician and official at the court of Córdoba, who used his place to support scholars, poets and communities. Today's word.
Your line: use your place. Today, make one introduction, write one recommendation, or open one door for someone who can't open it alone. Day nine hundred twenty.

921.title: Samuel HaNagid
921.hook: poet, scholar, and vizier of Granada
921.howItsDone: Samuel HaNagid's Hebrew poems are studied as part of the golden age of Hebrew poetry in Spain, and his title, Nagid, is remembered as the name for the leader of a Jewish community.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hasdai ibn Shaprut, the doctor at the court of Córdoba who backed scholars and poets. Your line was use your place. Did you open a door for someone? Today, a man who held a place and a pen at once. Day nine hundred twenty-one.

A small spice shop stands near a great man's house in Málaga. The shopkeeper is a refugee, a Jew who fled the fighting in Córdoba. He has beautiful handwriting and better Arabic, so a servant from the great house keeps coming in and asking him to write letters for her master. The letters are so good that the master, a vizier to the king of Granada, wants to know who is writing them. That, at least, is how the medieval chronicle tells it. The shopkeeper is Samuel ibn Naghrela. He will become the king's chief minister, lead armies, and write Hebrew poems about all of it. Jews will call him HaNagid.
screen: `A SPICE SHOP IN MÁLAGA.` → `LETTERS FOR THE VIZIER.` → `A REFUGEE CALLED TO COURT.`

segments.voice: Start with the title. Nagid is a Hebrew word the Bible uses for a leader. When God tells Samuel the prophet to anoint Saul, the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation renders it: "thou shalt anoint him to be prince over My people Israel." Prince there is nagid. So HaNagid means the leader, and Jews gave that title to the man who led their community in Granada. Now the double life. In the Muslim kingdom of Granada, Samuel rose from secretary to vizier, the king's chief minister. He also commanded Granada's armies in the field. And he wrote poems while he did it. Some are war poems, written on campaign, that thank God for being spared in battle. Some are about wine and gardens and friendship, in the style of Arabic poetry. Some are about death, sitting with the bones of old kings and wondering where they went. Some are written to his young son, teaching him to love learning. He gathered poems into books named after biblical ones: a son of Psalms, a son of Proverbs, a son of Ecclesiastes. Meanwhile, he wrote on Jewish law, supported students, and paid for copies of books for those who could not afford them. Statesman and poet, general and scholar. A shopkeeper who wrote well ended up shaping a kingdom, and wrote about it in the language of the Psalms. One person can hold two callings, and let each one feed the other. The pen made him a minister. The ministry gave the pen something to say.
screen: `NAGID: A BIBLICAL WORD FOR LEADER.` · then, large: `PRINCE OVER MY PEOPLE ISRAEL.` · `VIZIER AND GENERAL.` · `POEMS FROM THE BATTLEFIELD.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: two of your talents, side by side. Settle, and let your breath slow. Name one thing you are good at for work or duty. Organizing, fixing, caring for someone, numbers. Now name one thing you love that nobody pays you for. Singing, writing, cooking, drawing, walking. Hold them both. Is there one small way they could help each other this week? A note written with care, a meal that solves a problem, a song on the commute. Let one idea come. If you pray, you can give thanks in your own words for both gifts. The bell holds the time.
Samuel HaNagid. Samuel the leader: a refugee shopkeeper who became vizier of Granada, led its armies, and wrote Hebrew poems all the way. Today's word.
Your line: poet and statesman. Today, bring one of your quieter gifts into one of your duties, even for five minutes. Day nine hundred twenty-one.

922.title: Ibn Gabirol
922.hook: poet and philosopher; his poem Keter Malchut is read on Yom Kippur night
922.howItsDone: In some communities Keter Malchut is read privately or aloud on the night of Yom Kippur after the evening service, and several of Ibn Gabirol's poems appear in Jewish prayer books.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Samuel HaNagid, vizier, general and poet. Your line was poet and statesman. Did a quiet gift find its way into a duty? Today, a poet with no army and no palace, only a pen. Day nine hundred twenty-two.

Yom Kippur night. The long evening service is over, the synagogue is half empty, and the lights are low. In some communities, a few people stay on, open a prayer book to a long poem, and read it slowly, aloud or under their breath. It starts at the edge of the universe and ends with a single person admitting how small they are. The poem is called Keter Malchut, the royal crown. Its author was a poet in Spain who, by his own poems' account, was often lonely, sick, and at odds with the people around him, and who wrote as if the whole sky was his to describe. Today, Solomon ibn Gabirol.
screen: `YOM KIPPUR NIGHT, LIGHTS LOW.` → `A LONG POEM, READ SLOWLY.` → `KETER MALCHUT: THE ROYAL CROWN.`

segments.voice: Keter Malchut moves in three wide steps. First, it praises God with a string of names and attributes: God is one, God lives, God is great, God is light. Then it takes a tour of the universe as people of his time pictured it: the earth, the waters, the moon, the planets, the stars, sphere beyond sphere, each one described, each one a sign of its maker. And then, after all that size, it turns. The speaker looks at himself. A body made of dust, a short life, a list of wrongs. He confesses, and he asks for mercy. That turn is the heart of it. The bigger the sky gets, the more honest the person standing under it has to be. That is why it fits the night of Yom Kippur, the day of atonement. The poem leans on a much older song. Psalm one hundred four, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, says: "O LORD my God, Thou art very great; Thou art clothed with glory and majesty. Who coverest Thyself with light as with a garment." Ibn Gabirol takes that psalm's habit of looking at creation and praising, and stretches it across the whole sky as he knew it. He wrote other things too: philosophy about how the world comes from God, and personal poems about friendship, loneliness and grief. Some of his religious poems found their way into the prayer books of different communities. The title is the image to keep. A crown is something you place on a head. Here the poet weaves one out of words and offers it up, and then stands there, bareheaded, and tells the truth about himself.
screen: `PRAISE: GOD IS ONE, GOD IS LIGHT.` · `A TOUR OF THE WHOLE SKY.` · `THE TURN: AN HONEST CONFESSION.` · then, large: `LIGHT AS WITH A GARMENT.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: one short poem, read slowly. Settle, and let your breath slow. Take the line we just heard from Psalm one hundred four, or any short poem you love. Say the first line in your head. Pause. Let one image from it stay: light like a garment, a sky, a crown. Notice what it does to your breathing. Then say the next line, just as slowly. If you pray, you can let the words of the psalm be your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Ibn Gabirol. Solomon ibn Gabirol, poet and philosopher of Spain, whose long poem Keter Malchut moves from the whole sky to an honest confession. Today's word.
Your line: the royal crown. Today, look up once at the sky, and then, just as honestly, at one thing in yourself you'd rather not look at. Day nine hundred twenty-two.

923.title: Judah Halevi
923.hook: poet who wrote that his heart was in the east while he lived at the end of the west
923.howItsDone: Judah Halevi's poems to Zion are part of the kinot, the laments recited on Tisha B'Av in some communities, and his line about the heart in the east is quoted in Jewish writing about the land of Israel.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ibn Gabirol and his long poem, Keter Malchut. Your line was the royal crown. Did you look up at the sky, and then honestly at yourself? Today, another poet of Spain, whose heart lived somewhere else. Day nine hundred twenty-three.

A phone sits on a kitchen table in one city, open to the weather in another. Some people keep an app like that: the forecast for the place their parents were born, or where they grew up, or where someone they love lives now. They check it without thinking. Rain there. Sun there. Their body is here and part of their attention is always there. A poet in medieval Spain put something like that split into a short Hebrew poem. Today, Judah Halevi, the poet of the heart that faced east.
screen: `THE WEATHER IN ANOTHER CITY.` → `BODY HERE, ATTENTION THERE.` → `A POET WHOSE HEART FACED EAST.`

segments.voice: Judah Halevi lived in Christian and Muslim Spain, a doctor by trade, a celebrated poet, with friends, students, and a comfortable life. And yet one short poem of his opens with a split. Put plainly: my heart is in the east, and I am at the far end of the west. East is Jerusalem, the land of Israel. West is Spain, the edge of the map as he knew it. He goes on to ask how he can taste food or enjoy anything while Zion is in other hands and he is far away. He says that leaving all the good things of Spain would be easy, if only he could see the dust of the ruined sanctuary. That longing has deep roots. Psalm one hundred thirty-seven, sung by exiles by the rivers of Babylon, says in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget her cunning." Halevi takes that old vow and makes it personal and present tense. He also wrote a set of poems to Zion itself, addressing the land like a beloved. Some of them are recited on Tisha B'Av, the fast that mourns the Temple's destruction. Here is what lifts it beyond a poem. He decided to go. His poems describe the sea voyage, the waves, the fear, the ship. Tradition tells a legend that he reached the gates of Jerusalem, knelt to kiss the ground while reciting his poem to Zion, and was struck down by a passing rider. Nobody can confirm that story. But the poems that survive show a man who did not only long. He packed.
screen: `A COMFORTABLE LIFE IN SPAIN.` · `MY HEART IS IN THE EAST.` · then, large: `IF I FORGET THEE, O JERUSALEM.` · `HE DID NOT ONLY LONG. HE WENT.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: notice where your heart is. Settle, and let your breath slow. Feel where your body is: the chair, the floor, the room. Then ask, gently: where is my heart right now? It might be with a person, a place, a worry, a hope. Don't judge it. Just let it point. East, west, across town, across an ocean. Stay with that direction for a few breaths. Is there one small step toward it you could take this week? If you pray, you can bring that place or person into your prayer in your own words. The bell holds the time.
Judah Halevi. A poet and doctor in Spain who wrote that his heart was in the east, wrote poems to Zion, and set out to go there. Today's word.

924.title: The Kuzari
924.hook: Halevi's book: a king hears a philosopher, a Christian, a Muslim and a rabbi
924.howItsDone: The Kuzari is studied in yeshivas, adult classes and study groups as a classic of Jewish thought, often alongside the works of other medieval Jewish philosophers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Judah Halevi, whose heart was in the east. Your line was my heart in the east. Did you take one small step toward where your heart points? Today, the same man writes a book of questions. Day nine hundred twenty-four.

A king wakes up from a dream he can't shake. In it, an angel tells him: your intentions please your Creator, but your actions do not. He is a sincere man. He prays, he keeps the rituals of his people, he even serves at the altar himself. And still the dream comes back. So he does what a king can do. He summons people to explain the matter to him, one after another. A few days ago we heard about a letter sent to a faraway king of the Khazars. Judah Halevi sets his book at the Khazar court too, with an earlier king, generations before that letter. Today, the Kuzari: a book that begins with a man who doesn't know, and asks.
screen: `A DREAM THAT KEEPS COMING BACK.` → `GOOD INTENTIONS, WRONG ACTIONS.` → `THE KING SUMMONS TEACHERS.`

segments.voice: Halevi built his book on a tradition that a king of the Khazars and some of his people took up Judaism. He wrote it as a conversation. The king hears a philosopher, who tells him that God is far above caring about anyone's actions, and that what matters is to perfect your mind. Then a Christian scholar and a Muslim scholar each describe their faith. Then the king calls a rabbi. The rest of the book is the long talk between the king and the rabbi. To be clear about what kind of book this is: it is Halevi's case for Judaism, written by a Jew for Jews, at a time when Jews in Spain lived as a minority among Christian and Muslim neighbors. It is not neutral, and it does not pretend to be. What makes it interesting is how the rabbi starts. He does not open with a proof that the world was created, or an argument about the nature of God. He opens with a story. Put plainly: I believe in the God of Abraham, Isaac and Israel, who brought the children of Israel out of Egypt with signs and wonders, and gave them the Torah. That echoes the first of the Ten Commandments, which in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation begins: "I am the LORD thy God, who brought thee out of the land of Egypt." Halevi's point is that this faith starts with a memory a people shares, not with a philosopher's argument. Notice the shape of the frame, too. The king's problem is not belief. He is already devout. His problem is that his good intentions and his actions don't match. And the book begins because he is willing to say: I don't know. Explain it to me.
screen: `A KING WHO ASKS.` · `A CONVERSATION, NOT A LECTURE.` · then, large: `BROUGHT THEE OUT OF THE LAND OF EGYPT.` · `INTENTION AND ACTION MUST MEET.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: listen to several views on one question. Settle, and let your breath slow. Choose one question you care about. How to raise a child, how to spend Sunday, how to treat a difficult neighbor. Now, in your mind, let three different people you know answer it. Hear each one out, in their own words, without arguing back yet. Notice which answer surprises you, and what it would mean to take it seriously. If you pray, you can ask in your own words for an open mind. The bell holds the time.
The Kuzari. Judah Halevi's book in the form of a conversation: a king whose intentions are good but whose actions aren't right asks teachers, and a rabbi answers with a story. Today's word.
Your line: the king asks. Today, ask one real question of someone who sees the world differently, and listen to the whole answer before you reply. Day nine hundred twenty-four.

pairs: the God who brought Israel out of Egypt

myth: the Kuzari is written as a neutral survey of religions
it is Halevi's case for Judaism, written for Jews, and doesn't pretend to be neutral.
the king's problem in the dream is that he doesn't believe in God
he is already devout; the angel says his intentions please the Creator but his actions do not.
the rabbi opens with a story, not a proof
he begins with the God who brought Israel out of Egypt and gave the Torah.

fork.setup: you are the king. an angel says your intentions are good but your actions are not. you are already devout. what do you do?
options: ignore the dream; you already pray.
summon teachers and ask them to explain.
change nothing and hope it stops.
fork.reveal: the king summons a philosopher, a Christian scholar, a Muslim scholar and then a rabbi. The whole book begins because he is willing to ask.

original.note: Hebrew: 'the Khazar', the name of Judah Halevi's book.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Kuzari is a history book about the Khazars.
what it means: it is a conversation built on a tradition about a Khazar king, used to make Halevi's case for Judaism.
what a scholar hears: the rabbi opens with shared memory, the Exodus and the giving of the Torah, rather than a philosophical proof.
